title: Chapter 227 – Han's Porridge
html:
[The Wall – Qinghe]

Qinghe has cooked for a hundred and one years, and she has never once cooked for a dead man.

She stands at the long iron stove in the Wall's great kitchen at the hour before dawn, with a wooden spoon in her hand and a pot of porridge at her elbow, and listens to the room. This is how she has always done it. She listens, and the room tells her what it needs. The fire says it is a little low. The pot says it is a little thick. The floor, under her broad bare feet, says that someone has spilled milk by the pantry door. She has not needed her eyes for a long time.

She does not need them now to know that the chair at the end of the long table is empty.

It is Han's chair. It has been Han's for sixty years. It is a plain oak thing with a high back and one short leg, and every morning at the first bell he has lowered himself into it with a grunt and a creak of knees and said, in the voice of a man who has been rehearsing it since the previous day: good morning, Qinghe. Is there any porridge?

And she has said: there is always porridge.

And that has been the whole of their conversation, most mornings, for sixty years.

She stirs the pot. She tilts her head. In the silence of the great vaulted room there is a sound she has been trying not to hear: a long, slow, rattling breath, drawn in and let out, in a chamber on the second floor of the east tower. It is coming from an old man in a narrow bed. It is the sound of a candle burning to the socket.

"Not yet," says Qinghe, to the pot.

It does not answer.

---

He is a hundred and eight years old.

She goes up at first light, with a bowl in her hands, because she cannot think of anything else to do. The east tower stair is steep and narrow and smells of tallow and old stone. She climbs it with the slow patience of a woman who has done it ten thousand times and has never once grudged the steps. At the top there is a door, and a lamp, and a small, high, sparely furnished room.

Mo Yan is already there.

She sits on a stool by the bed, in her gray cloak, with her iron-gray hair cut short at the jaw and her hands folded in her lap. She is fifty-eight. She has been sitting here since midnight. She looks up when the door opens, and her closed-fist face softens, a very little, and she puts a finger to her lips.

Qinghe sets the bowl on the table.

The man in the bed is very small. It is the thing that surprises her, every time. He was a big man, once. He was a giant, with shoulders like a doorframe and a laugh that rattled the plates. Now he lies under a gray blanket with his white beard spread on his chest and his enormous hands folded over the hilt of a sword, and he is hardly longer than a child. His face is yellow and sunken. His eyes are closed. His breath comes in long, slow, labored draws, with a dreadful quiet between each.

"He was awake an hour ago," Mo Yan says, softly. "He asked if you'd come."

"I was making the porridge."

"I told him."

"What did he say?"

"He said that was all right." A faint, wry curl of the mouth. "He said there was always porridge."

Qinghe's eyes sting.

She is a woman of a hundred and one. She has buried two husbands and a son. She has stood on the Wall in the worst winter of the century and fed three thousand men from a single pot. She does not weep easily. But she lowers herself onto the end of the bed, with a creak of old knees, and takes the huge cold hand in both of hers, and for a moment she cannot speak at all.

---

"Qinghe."

The voice is a thread.

She leans down. His eyes have opened. They are pale and faded, like old rope, and they swim slowly, and fix on her face with a look of enormous effort.

"There you are," he says.

"I'm here."

"Is it morning?"

"It's just morning."

"Good." A long wheeze. "I never could abide the dark."

"I know."

"You've no shadow."

"I know that too."

"I always meant to ask." His mouth twitches. "It's not a bad look, on you. I thought you'd go to pieces. A woman who's lost her shadow. It's a thing that happens to witches."

"I'm not a witch."

"You make a very good porridge."

"That's not the same."

"It's near enough." His fingers close, a very little, on hers. "I'd like to eat. If it's not too much trouble."

She does not trust herself to speak. She lifts the bowl and the spoon, and holds a mouthful to his lips, and he opens them like a child. He swallows. He chews, slowly, with his eyes shut, with the grave attention of a man tasting something for the last time. A thin trickle of milk runs into his beard.

"Cinnamon," he says.

"A little."

"You always put in too much."

"I put in exactly enough."

"Aye." His lips curve. "That's what I mean."

He eats three spoonfuls. Then he shakes his head, and she sets the bowl aside, and the room is very quiet. A pale square of light has crept across the floor from the high window. In it, dust turns slowly.

"Mo Yan," says Han.

"I'm here, old man."

"Come closer. I can't see you."

She comes. She kneels at the bedside, and he turns his head on the pillow and studies her, with those pale unfocused eyes, as if she were a map of a country he had once known well.

"You grew up," he says.

"I had help."

"You did." A breath. "You were nine. You stood at the gate with a bundle. You said, take me to Wenyuan. I thought you were the stubbornest creature I had ever seen."

"I probably was."

"You still are." The old mouth quirks. "It's a fine thing in a woman. I never cared for the other kind."

She laughs. It cracks in her throat.

"I want you to do something," says Han.

"Anything."

"The sword." His hands move on the hilt. "It's no good to me. I've nobody to leave it to. I thought of the lad. Pebble. He'd have been a good captain, if he'd stayed." A wheeze. "But he's up the Road, and I don't suppose I'll see him again."

"You might."

"I'm a hundred and eight, girl. I've seen what there is to see." He closes his eyes. "Give it to someone who stays. That's all I ask. It doesn't matter who. A boy from the lower court. A girl from the kitchen. Someone who'll hold the gate when it needs holding, and not make a speech about it."

"I'll find them."

"I know you will."

"Han—"

"And tell Wenyuan—" He stops. His brow furrows. "Tell him I never did like his tea."

Mo Yan makes a small broken sound.

"I'll tell him," she says.

"He'll know what I mean."

"I know he will."

"Good." A long exhale. "That's all, then."

He does not say anything more.

---

It takes an hour.

Qinghe sits through all of it, with his hand in hers, and the pale light moving across the floor.

She remembers the first morning.

It is not a thing she does often. She is not a woman who lives in the past; there is too much porridge to make. But the room is very quiet, and the hand in hers is very cold, and somewhere between one long breath and the next the years slip loose and she is twenty-eight again, standing in the doorway of a ruined kitchen in the first winter of the war.

There is no roof. There is snow on the floor. A cauldron hangs over a fire of broken chair-legs, and in front of it, sitting on an upturned bucket with his sword across his knees, is the biggest man she has ever seen. He is perhaps thirty. His beard is black. His hands are the size of shovels. He is eating something out of a tin cup with an expression of such profound suspicion that she almost laughs.

"What is it?" she asks.

"Soup."

"What's in it?"

"I haven't the faintest idea." He looks at her over the cup. "I found it in the pot. I thought it best not to ask."

"There's a rat in it."

"Is there?" He peers into the cup. "Well, that explains the texture."

She does laugh then, she cannot help it, a loud ugly honk that startles a sparrow off the rafters. And the big man looks up at her, startled, and then, slowly, as if he has not done it in a long time, he grins.

It is the best thing she has ever seen.

"I'm the cook," she says. "Since this morning. They told me the last one ran off."

"Did he?"

"With the good knives."

"Sensible man." He sets down the cup. "I'm the commander. Since yesterday. They told me the last one died."

"Did he?"

"Of the soup, I rather think."

They look at each other across the ruined kitchen. The snow drifts in through the roof. And Qinghe, who is twenty-eight and widowed and has not smiled in a month, finds that she has crossed the floor, and picked up the cauldron's ladle, and is stirring.

"Sit," she says. "I'll start again."

He sits.

That was the first morning. There were twenty-three thousand more.

She does not speak. She does not pray. She listens, as she has always done, to the shape of the room, and she hears the long breaths grow longer and the pauses between them stretch like a rope drawn tight. She hears Mo Yan's heartbeat, steady, strong, a little fast. She hears the Seam beyond the window, humming low, a thin sullen chord. She hears, at the very end of everything, the small dry sound of an old man's breath going out of him for the last time, and not coming back.

Nobody moves.

After a while Mo Yan reaches out and closes his eyes, with two fingers, as one smooths a child's brow. She sits back on her heels. She draws a long shuddering breath.

"There," she says, to nobody. "That's done."

Qinghe lays the huge hand on the hilt, and folds the fingers, one by one.

"Aye," she says. "That's done."

She rises. Her knees ache. She goes to the window, and looks out, and sees the Wall in the first gold light: the long black rampart, the beacon fires burning low, the sentries stamping and blowing on their hands. The sun is coming up behind the east tower. Far to the north, along the line of the Seam, a thin pearly glow is spreading up the sky.

Odd, she thinks.

She tilts her head. She listens.

The hum has changed.

---

They wash him in the late morning, in the small stone room behind the infirmary.

It is Little Mei who insists. She is fifty-nine now, a brisk gray-curled woman with a healer's apron and a voice that carries, and she has stayed at the Wall since the night of the first tremor, because, she says, a place with only one physician is a place in want of two. She has a kettle of warm water and a pile of clean linen. She has rolled her sleeves to the elbow. She stands at the foot of the table, where the old man lies under a sheet, and looks at him for a long moment with her head on one side.

"I never met him properly," she says. "Not when he was well."

"He was loud," says Qinghe.

"I'm told."

"He sang in the bath."

"Did he?"

"Terribly." Qinghe takes a cloth from the pile. "The whole east tower knew the words to The Maid of the Gray Bridge. I suspect he was the only man alive who thought it was in tune."

Little Mei laughs, softly, and takes up a second cloth.

They work without speaking. It is a thing Qinghe has done before, many times, and she finds that her hands know the order of it. The face, first. The arms. The great scarred chest, with its map of old wounds, each one a year, each one a name. The long legs, thin now, the knees swollen like knots in rope. She wipes the fingers one by one. She sets them back on the hilt.

"There's something," says Little Mei.

She has been smoothing the sleeve of the old white shirt, and her fingers have stopped. She draws out, from the cuff, a small flat folded square of paper, much creased. It has been there a long time. The edges are soft as cloth.

"It's addressed," she says.

Qinghe takes it.

She cannot read it. She has not needed to; she has her ears. But she feels the fine ridges of the ink under her thumb, and she holds it out to the younger woman, and says, "Read it, would you?"

Little Mei unfolds it carefully.

"For Pebble," she reads. Her voice is slow. "When he comes down. Or for whoever finds this if he doesn't."

"Go on."

"I wasn't a good teacher. I shouted a great deal and I never said what I meant. So I'll say it here, where I can't make a hash of it. You stayed. When the rest of them ran, you stayed. I watched you hold a torch on that parapet with the stones coming down, and I thought: there is a man." She stops. Swallows. "I never told you. I'm telling you now. You were the best soldier I ever commanded. Be kind to yourself. It's a thing I never learned."

She stops.

"Is that all?"

"There's a line at the bottom." Little Mei's voice cracks. "P.S. The sword is yours. Don't let them give it to a committee."

For a long time, neither of them speaks.

Qinghe folds the paper along its old creases. She tucks it, quite gently, into the breast of her own apron. "I'll keep it," she says. "Until he comes."

"He may not."

"He may not." She smooths the front of her apron. "But he's a stubborn lad. I've a feeling about him."

"What kind of feeling?"

"The kind," says Qinghe, "that comes from listening to a great deal of porridge."

Little Mei looks at her.

Then she laughs, a wet, helpless, honking laugh that shakes her whole body, and puts her hand over her mouth, and cannot stop. And Qinghe, who has been holding herself very straight since dawn, feels something in her chest give way, and finds that she is laughing too. They stand together in the little stone room, two old women with wet cloths and a dead man between them, laughing until the tears run down their faces.

It is the best funeral rite she has ever attended. When it is over, they finish the washing, and wrap him in the old gray banner of the Wall, and Qinghe sews the seam herself with a needle and thread she keeps in her apron for the purpose. She makes the stitches small and even. It is, she thinks, the last thing she will ever make for him, and she makes it the way she makes everything, with her whole attention, and without a word.

---

They bury him at noon, on the rampart, under a plain gray stone.

It is a small ceremony. The Wall is not a place for pomp. A hundred soldiers in their gray tunics stand at attention in the cold wind, and the Sect's Elder Chao Wen's successor, a thin young woman named Ruo, reads the prayer for the dead in a clear voice. The priests of the Hall of Ten Thousand Names have sent a wreath of white lilies, which are already wilting. A child from the school sings one verse of an old marching song, off-key, and loses her nerve, and is lifted onto the shoulders of a sergeant who has gone suddenly rigid with the effort of not weeping.

Wenyuan does not attend.

He cannot. He is the tower. But he is there, all the same: a pale presence at the edge of everything, a coolness in the air, a faint hum in the stone underfoot. Qinghe feels him, as she has felt him every day for seventy-four years, and when the first spadeful of earth falls on the plain pine coffin she hears, in the back of her mind, very softly, a voice that does not use air.

He hated my tea, it says.

Aye.

I made it the way my mother did.

It tasted like boiled grass.

I know. A pause. I shall miss him terribly.

So shall I.

He called me "boy" until I was seventy.

He called us all that.

It was kind. The voice, wry, tender, immensely tired, fades. Tell Mo Yan she is doing very well.

Qinghe closes her eyes.

---

The stone is set. The speeches are done. The soldiers file off the rampart in ranks, with their helmets under their arms, and Mo Yan stands alone at the grave with a handful of earth and a face like a shut door. Qinghe waits. She is good at waiting. She stands a pace behind, with her hands folded in her apron, and watches the wind pull at the girl's gray hair.

"It's strange," says Mo Yan, at last.

"What is?"

"I thought I'd feel it more." She opens her fingers and lets the earth fall. "I've been braced for this for years. I thought when it came, it would hit like a wall. And instead it's just—" She searches for the word. "Quiet."

"It does that."

"Does it get louder?"

"Sometimes." Qinghe considers. "Mostly it gets easier to carry. Not lighter. But you grow a back for it."

Mo Yan almost smiles.

"You sound like him."

"I should. I'd sixty years of listening."

"I'm going up," says Mo Yan.

She says it quite calmly, to the grave, with her back to Qinghe. The wind pulls at her cloak. A hawk hangs in the air above the northern plain, motionless, as if painted on the sky.

"I thought you might be."

"Did you?"

"I've been listening to you not say it for a month."

Mo Yan makes a sound that might be a laugh. "I made a promise," she says. "Not to Jian. To myself. I told myself that when the old man was gone, when there was nobody left who needed me, I would take the Hundred Stairs and go and find out what happened to the people I love." She turns. Her eyes are dry and fierce. "I've waited fifty years. I think I've waited long enough."

"The bell?"

"Comes with me."

"The Seam?"

"Wenyuan holds it. He always has. He doesn't need me." A breath. "He needs someone who can sing the Cradle, and Lan Xiu can do that. She's been doing it for thirty years."

"And what will I do?"

"You'll cook."

"That," says Qinghe, "is what I was afraid of."

Mo Yan crosses the stones in three strides and wraps both arms around the old woman, hard, in the silent clumsy fierce way of someone who has never learned to do it softly. She smells of wood smoke and cold air. Qinghe holds her. Her own arms, thin and strong and shadowless, close round the girl's back.

"You'll eat before you go," she says into her shoulder. "Something hot. And a loaf for the road."

"I will."

"And you'll write."

"I'll write."

"I'll know if you don't."

"I know you will."

They stand together in the wind. A hawk circles high over the northern plain. The beacon fires on the rampart gutter and pop. And in the pocket of Mo Yan's cloak, Qinghe hears, very faint, a small clear voice.

Mo Yan.

"I'm here, Sera."

Look up.

Mo Yan looks up.

It takes Qinghe a moment longer. She has no eyes for the sky; she has not needed them. But there is a change in the air, a lifting, a quickening of pressure, and the hairs on her arms rise. She turns her face to the north. She listens, with her whole body, as she has listened to every room she has ever stood in.

She hears, for the first time in seventy-four years, absolutely nothing.

The Seam has stopped humming.

---

They are on the northern parapet in a quarter of an hour: Mo Yan, and Qinghe, and Lan Xiu, who has come at a run from the Sect's quarters with her gray braid flying, and the sentries, who have stopped pacing, and a hundred soldiers in the courtyard below, who have come out of the barracks in their shirtsleeves and are standing with their faces upturned.

The sky is lit.

It is lit all across the north, from horizon to horizon, with a pale silver radiance like the inside of a pearl. The crack that has hung there for six hundred years has widened. It is no longer a scar but a wound, a great gaping rent, miles across, with ragged edges of white fire. And through it, high up, impossibly distant, something is showing.

It is a roof.

Qinghe cannot see it. She does not need to. She hears the sentries breathe in. She hears Lan Xiu's whisper, hoarse with awe: a dome. A dome of glass. And she hears, beneath it, a sound she has not heard since the night the Orchard burned: a vast, slow, tidal murmur, like the singing of a very large and very happy crowd.

"What is it?" she says.

"The Door," says Mo Yan. Her voice is thin. "I think it's the Door. It's opened. It's—" She stops. "Oh."

"Oh, what?"

"There are people."

Qinghe turns her head.

"Thousands of them. Millions." Mo Yan's voice cracks. "They're in the sky. They're hanging in the air, in rows, like—like stars. Like threads on a loom. They're all holding hands. They're all—" She chokes. "They're all smiling."

The Refused, thinks Qinghe.

Seventy-four years of them. Woven into the warp.

"There's a woman," says Mo Yan. "Near the front. With a scar on her chin. She's looking down." A sob. "She's waving."

"Do you know her?"

"I've never seen her before in my life."

But her voice is the voice of someone who has just recognized a face in a crowd, and does not know how, and cannot stop looking.

In her pocket, quite clear, the white bell begins to ring.

Mo Yan, says Sera.

"I'm here."

It's calling you.

"I know."

You mustn't go.

"I'm not going anywhere." Mo Yan's voice is hard and low. "I'm fifty-eight. I've a funeral to finish."

It's not asking you to go. The voice in the bell is very small. It's asking you to look.

Qinghe opens her mouth to say something, anything, and finds that she has nothing to say.

She stands on the rampart in her patched apron, a short broad old woman with no shadow, and listens to the sky sing. And somewhere very far below her feet, in a tower of living stone, a blind man sits upright in a chair with his hands folded, and does not breathe.

Wenyuan, she thinks.

I hear it, he answers, from a great way off. It is not the Bloom.

Who, then?

Someone is shouting down the Road, says the Keystone of the Wall. Someone who has reached the Door. A long pause. They are shouting for the Nine.
